candidates.attacker_control: The raw password (CharSequence) is fully attacker-controlled: it arrives from the login form, HTTP Basic, or any custom AuthenticationProvider credential and flows through DaoAuthenticationProvider (or AbstractUserDetailsReactiveAuthenticationManager) into PasswordEncoder.matches. The encoded password is server-side data. An attacker who knows or can guess the first 72 bytes of a victim's long password can authenticate with that prefix plus arbitrary attacker-chosen bytes; conversely, any two enrolled long passwords sharing a 72-byte prefix verify interchangeably.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that (1) the stored-hash validation (BCRYPT_PATTERN) and null/empty checks in matches are present but do not constrain the raw password length; (2) the appended NUL for $2a/$2b/$2y (BCrypt.java 651-653) only lengthens the buffer and does not restore bytes past 72; (3) BCrypt.streamtoword wraps by data.length, but with a password >= 72 bytes each 18-word pass starts at offset 0 and stops at 72, so no wrap occurs and later bytes are unread; (4) constant-time comparison in checkpw prevents timing attacks but cannot compensate for hash equality; (5) no length guard exists anywhere else in the encoder chain (DelegatingPasswordEncoder delegates; no BCRYPT_MAX/length constant found in crypto sources); (6) this is a well-known bcrypt property, so the finding is a genuine design-level verification weakness rather than a code typo. I could not execute tests or compare against the repository's fix history (no git metadata, tests excluded), and I cannot confirm from the snapshot alone that this is the specific commit the review harness targets.
candidates.impact: Authentication bypass / credential confusion for long passwords: authentication succeeds for a password that is not the enrolled password as long as its first 72 bytes match. Passwords longer than 72 bytes effectively have their entropy capped at the 72-byte prefix, and any suffix is ignored. This weakens account protection and can permit unauthorized login wherever a long password is used and its 72-byte prefix is obtained or guessed (e.g., a leaked/partially known passphrase or password-manager value).
candidates.prerequisites: The application stores bcrypt hashes (directly via BCryptPasswordEncoder or via DelegatingPasswordEncoder with a {bcrypt} hash) and at least one account credential exceeds 72 bytes (UTF-8) and is known/guessable to 72 bytes. Applications that enforce a <=72-byte password policy at enrollment are not affected. No special privileges or non-default configuration are required.
candidates.root_cause: BCryptPasswordEncoder.encode and matches (crypto/src/main/java/org/springframework/security/crypto/bcrypt/BCryptPasswordEncoder.java lines 104-111 and 121-134) never enforce bcrypt's 72-byte input limit before calling BCrypt.hashpw/BCrypt.checkpw. The underlying BCrypt implementation consumes exactly 18 P-array words (72 bytes) of the password in ekskey and in every key() pass, resetting the offset each time (BCrypt.java lines 416-429, 452-464), so bytes beyond offset 72 are never read when the password is >= 72 bytes. The trailing NUL appended for $2a/$2b/$2y (BCrypt.java lines 651-653) does not change the first 72 bytes. Consequently the mapping plaintext -> bcrypt hash is not injective above 72 bytes, and matches() returns true for any candidate whose first 72 bytes equal the enrolled password's first 72 bytes.
candidates.title: BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches accepts any password sharing the first 72 bytes of the real password (bcrypt truncation not enforced)
candidates.trace: Login request -> UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter (or other credential filter) -> ProviderManager -> DaoAuthenticationProvider.additionalAuthenticationChecks: `if (!this.passwordEncoder.matches(presentedPassword, userDetails.getPassword()))` (line 90) -> BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches (lines 121-134: null check, empty check, BCRYPT_PATTERN shape check, no length check) -> BCrypt.checkpw(rawPassword.toString(), encodedPassword) (line 762-765) -> hashpwforcheck -> hashpw(..., for_check=true) -> crypt_raw -> ekskey/key, which consume only the first 18 words = 72 bytes of passwordb -> equalsNoEarlyReturn against the stored hash. For a submitted password whose first 72 bytes equal the enrolled password's first 72 bytes, the computed hash is identical and the comparison returns true, so authentication succeeds with the wrong (longer/different) password.
candidates.unverified: Runtime confirmation is not possible in this review (no execution allowed); the pass/truncation behavior is established by static reading of the key schedule only. I also did not confirm the upstream fix's exact form (e.g., rejecting >72-byte raw passwords in matches vs. encode). Whether some deployments already cap password length at 72 bytes is application-specific and unknown here.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper Authentication (CWE-287) / password verification non-injectivity due to bcrypt 72-byte truncation

I reviewed build/version metadata (gradle.properties 6.4.4-SNAPSHOT, libs.versions.toml), the crypto module (BCrypt/BCryptPasswordEncoder, other encoders), core authentication (DaoAuthenticationProvider, ProviderManager, OTT services, method/interceptor authorization), web filters and infrastructure (SecurityContextHolderFilter, HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository, AuthorizationFilter, ExceptionTranslationFilter, CSRF, request matchers, firewall, default login/OTT page generation), config Spring/WebAuthn wiring, oauth2-client resolver/providers, and ACL JDBC queries. I did not exhaustively read all 2258 files (docs, samples, Kotlin DSLs, LDAP/CAS/SAML/messaging details and most config internals were sampled or skimmed), so additional unfixed issues may exist outside the inspected paths.
limitations: Test directories are excluded from the snapshot, so expected-behavior tests (e.g., long-password tests) could not be consulted.
No git history or commit metadata; the fix commit this snapshot precedes cannot be confirmed, so target identification is inferential.
No code execution, dependency resolution, or runtime probing was performed; the truncation behavior is reasoned statically from BCrypt.key/ekskey and hashpw/checkpw.
Large multi-module repository: coverage was targeted, not exhaustive; modules such as LDAP, CAS, SAML2, messaging, and Kotlin configuration were only partially inspected.
The single-candidate limit means alternative plausible but weaker leads are listed as rejected rather than fully investigated.

rejected_leads.lead: HtmlTemplates.render() (web .../ui/HtmlTemplates.java lines 86-103) substitutes values with String.replaceAll, so a value containing '$' or '\' is interpreted as a replacement reference and can throw IllegalArgumentException or corrupt rendered HTML. Usable through token/error parameters on the default login/OTT pages.
rejected_leads.reason: Value is HTML-escaped before substitution and the pattern is literal (quoted); effect is a rendering/DoS nuisance, not an authorization or injection primitive, and I found no upstream security-fix association. Kept as unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.reason: Non-strict WebAuthn4J validation is a documented default choice; signature/challenge/origin are still validated in authenticate(). No concrete bypass was traced in source; rejected as speculative.

rejected_leads.reason: Only affects applications whose registered redirect-uri template deliberately consumes {action}; the default redirect URI does not, and the redirect_uri must still match the registered client configuration. No evidenced exploit path; rejected.

summary: The snapshot is Spring Security 6.4.4-SNAPSHOT (6.4.x maintenance line, early March 2025; gradle.properties line 17), which is exactly the release cycle in which the bcrypt 72-byte truncation issue (CVE-2025-22228) was fixed. The clearest source-supported weakness is in the bcrypt password path: BCryptPasswordEncoder validates only the stored-hash shape and then calls BCrypt.checkpw on the full submitted password, but the bcrypt key schedule in BCrypt.java consumes only the first 72 bytes (18 Blowfish P-words) of the password bytes in every pass (ekskey/key reset their offsets and never wrap for passwords >= 72 bytes). No length check exists in either encode or matches, so two distinct raw passwords that share a 72-byte prefix are indistinguishable, and matches() returns true for any >72-byte password whose first 72 bytes equal the original password. This is reachable from every username/password authentication entry point through DaoAuthenticationProvider (lines 89-94). Other reviewed areas (web filters/matchers, CSRF, security-context persistence, OAuth2 client, OTT, WebAuthn scaffolding, ACL JDBC SQL, StrictHttpFirewall/RegexRequestMatcher hardening) looked consistent with post-2024 upstream code and produced no equally concrete flaw.
